title: Compare and Contrast Common Data Destruction and Disposal Methods

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Retired drives and devices can still contain passwords, customer records, personal data, financial information, and proprietary material. Disposal must make that information unrecoverable to the required standard.
sections.callout: Reuse it → wipe it; destroy it → physically destroy it; outsource it → verify it.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When media will be reused, recycled, transferred, or destroyed, select a method that protects the data, preserves the device only when required, and satisfies organizational, regulatory, and environmental rules.

sections.title: Physical Destruction of Hard Drives
paragraphs: Physical destruction is appropriate when storage media no longer needs to remain usable.

entries.title: Drilling
paragraphs: Punctures and damages key drive components so the device cannot operate normally.

entries.title: Shredding
paragraphs: Mechanically reduces storage devices to small fragments.

entries.title: Degaussing
paragraphs: Uses a strong magnetic field to disrupt information on magnetic media such as hard disk drives and tapes. It is not a general solution for flash-based SSDs.
entries.recognitionCue: Magnetic storage plus magnetic erasure → degaussing.

entries.title: Incineration
paragraphs: Uses extreme heat to destroy the storage media physically.

table.caption: Match the destruction method to the clue

sections.title: Recycling or Repurposing Best Practices
paragraphs: If media will remain usable, sanitize its prior information appropriately before reuse, transfer, or recycling.

entries.title: Erasing/Wiping
paragraphs: Intentionally sanitizes stored information so previous data is difficult or impractical to recover.
entries.recognitionCue: Reuse the drive → wipe it first.

entries.title: Low-Level Formatting
paragraphs: Represents deeper storage initialization or erasure than ordinary filesystem formatting. Modern devices often rely on secure-erase or manufacturer sanitization functions rather than literal low-level reconstruction.

entries.title: Standard Formatting
paragraphs: Creates or recreates a filesystem such as NTFS or exFAT but should not automatically be treated as guaranteed secure destruction.

sections.title: Standard Formatting vs. Secure Wiping
paragraphs: Standard formatting rebuilds filesystem structures. Secure wiping is specifically intended to sanitize information that existed previously.
sections.callout: Prepare a filesystem → format; securely remove old data → wipe.

table.caption: Choose based on whether the media must remain usable

entries.title: Third-Party Vendor
paragraphs: An outside company hired to destroy storage, recycle hardware, or dispose of equipment. Outsourcing does not remove the data owner's responsibility.
entries.recognitionCue: Outside company handles disposal → third-party vendor.

entries.title: Certification of Destruction/Recycling
paragraphs: Documentation showing that media or equipment was destroyed, sanitized, or recycled as required.
entries.recognitionCue: Auditable proof the work occurred → certificate.

sections.title: Chain of Responsibility
paragraphs: When a vendor handles media, maintain secure control and documentation from pickup through final destruction or recycling.
sections.callout: Do not lose control of the data merely because someone else destroys it.

sections.title: Regulatory and Environmental Requirements

entries.title: Regulatory Requirements
paragraphs: Laws, regulations, contracts, or policy may specify retention periods, approved destruction methods, privacy safeguards, and disposal records.

entries.title: Environmental Requirements
paragraphs: Electronic equipment may contain materials requiring approved e-waste recyclers, disposal providers, and environmental procedures rather than ordinary trash.

sections.callout: Secure disposal and responsible disposal are both required.

sections.title: Disposal Decision Model
bullets: Determine whether the media must remain usable.
Classify data sensitivity and the required sanitization standard.
Choose wiping for reuse or approved physical destruction when reuse is prohibited.
Use media-appropriate methods; degaussing applies to magnetic media.
If outsourcing, verify the vendor, chain of responsibility, and certification.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Keep media but sanitize it → erasing/wiping
Proof of destruction → certification of destruction/recycling

sections.title: Objective 2.9 Exam Trap
bullets: Deleting file references is not the same as securely wiping underlying data.
Standard formatting rebuilds a filesystem; secure wiping sanitizes prior information.
Degaussing applies to magnetic media and should not be the automatic answer for SSDs.
If the device must remain usable, do not physically destroy it.
A third-party vendor performs the work; a certificate proves the required work occurred.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
sections.callout: Reuse it → wipe it; destroy it → physically destroy it; outsource it → verify it.
